title: A Thousand Thoughts

Sitting in a dark room with strangers is a radical act!

title: Ausente
text: Through my work, I question how we negotiate our existence and our agency within the systems we inhabit. I am interested in the relationship between individuals and the natural, social, political, technological, and digital structures that surround us. Systems identify, classify, and represent us. They organize bodies, territories, information, and memory, and can also produce exclusion or disappearance.
speaker: Paolo Almario
source: Paolo Almario, artist statement (paoloalmario.com)

title: Ausente
text: I construct machines, algorithms, protocols, and situations and allow them to act: to classify, accumulate, transform, reveal, deteriorate, erase. Through these operations, processes that might remain abstract become physical, temporal, perceptible. A system can be experienced through what it does.
speaker: Paolo Almario
source: Paolo Almario, artist statement (paoloalmario.com)

title: Ausente
text: I do not try to resolve these tensions. I try to create conditions in which they become perceptible and can be experienced. What returns throughout the practice is this negotiation: between individual and system, agency and constraint, presence and disappearance.

source: Paolo Almario, artist statement (paoloalmario.com)

title: Ausente
text: The work asks how the collective gestures of a society align into a system that decides who is to be excluded, targeted, eliminated, and how today's technological tools extend that capacity for segregation: documenting, locating and targeting individuals under cover of notions such as sovereignty.

title: catástrofe orquestra #1 (Ato I)
text: The history of humanity is like a great battle of materialities. When I received the invitation from the Bienal, it was a great opportunity to reflect on the materials I’ve been researching and how they might collide with one another, generating friction. The matchboxes that carry fire. Coal, which is essentially a fossilized, burned tree; which fueled industrial production in the past century; which brought us to our current technological model—driven and shaped by the historical rhythms that fire (and water) have created over time. In catástrofe orquestra #1 (Ato I), I am interested in the violent act of the coal pendulums being dropped onto the drum as a representation of this historical thread.

source: "Catastrophe orchestra: an interview with Antonio Társis", Fundação Bienal de São Paulo

title: catástrofe orquestra #1 (Ato I)

One thing overlapping another, like a massive fire having a domino effect or a large orchestra in which each instrument has its own function and note. The catastrophe ceases to be an isolated event and comes to be seen as a functioning system, governing our lives at every moment.

text: Dissent appears through the mechanical rhythms and the tension they create. The installation plays with the contrast between human rhythm and machine-driven rhythm, reflecting how our cultural and environmental rhythms are disrupted by modern life. The automated beat becomes a subtle form of questioning: how do we hold onto heritage in a rapidly changing world?
speaker: Dinoj Mahendranathan
source: The Art of Listening: In Conversation with Dinoj M, ARTRA Magazine

title: Circles of Rhythm and Rains
text: Renewal is at the core of the work. The installation continuously shifts, rhythms build, fade, restart, and reinterlock. This cyclical movement parallels how cultural practices evolve and regenerate with time. I believe this work will let the audience feel rhythm as a living thing; it remembers, it contests, and it changes.
speaker: Dinoj Mahendranathan
source: The Art of Listening: In Conversation with Dinoj M, ARTRA Magazine

title: Circles of Rhythm and Rains
text: It's also about archiving, especially endangered bird sounds, because sound is one of the first things we lose when ecosystems collapse.

title: Codex Virtualis_Genesis
text: Artificial intelligence, in this case, acts as a meta-researcher, helping us find patterns and identify emergencies at different levels of phenomena. Over time, we have positioned it as a creative agent, capable of producing subjectivity.

title: Codex Virtualis_Genesis

speaker: Interspecifics
source: 'Artificial intelligence as a meta-researcher', Ars Electronica Blog interview (2021)

title: Codex Virtualis_Genesis

title: Codex Virtualis_Genesis

title: Codex Virtualis_Genesis

speaker: Interspecifics

title: Collective Body

title: Collective Body
text: I was asking myself, “What does this mean for our embodied selves? What does it mean for the way we express ourselves physically if we’re only going to be these avatars? How can we represent ourselves differently in the virtual space? How could I create something that actually used the virtual to bring us together in real life?”
speaker: Sarah Silverblatt-Buser
source: The Dance Enthusiast Asks, interview by Sarah Cecilia Bukowski (2025)

title: Collective Body
text: I wanted to find something that could question this potential virtual future and remind us of the importance of physicality in the sense of how our bodies express and represent our ingrained histories that we don’t necessarily speak about. So I wanted to do something that would allow us to meet each other through movement.
speaker: Sarah Silverblatt-Buser
source: The Dance Enthusiast Asks, interview by Sarah Cecilia Bukowski (2025)

title: Collective Body

title: Corpus Nil
text: And if there’s an aim in this artwork – and more generally in my whole body of works – it is exactly that: to create a performative experience that cannot be immediately rationalised, but instead hits you fast and hard so that it remains vivid in your memories.

source: Ars Electronica Blog, '“Corpus Nil”: A Performance by Man and Artificial Intelligence' (interview, 4 September 2017)

title: Corpus Nil

title: Corpus Nil

title: Crossings
text: Throughout my adolescence in Morocco, stories of migrants drowning at sea became regular on the news. In my eyes, these stories were constant reminders of deep-rooted social injustice.

title: Crossings
text: As a Moroccan, I felt very ashamed and felt some kind of responsibility to fight against the violent treatment of sub-Saharan migrants, who because of their “clandestine” status are deprived of basic human rights.

source: Nahrain Al-Mousawi, 'When we spoke to Leila Alaoui on tackling taboos in art', Al Jazeera, 19 July 2015

title: Crossings
text: This experience nurtured the idea of an immersive audiovisual experience through which to share personal stories of migration and re-enact the disturbing sensations of the journey. I truly wanted to do a project that humanised and dignified the migrants.

source: Nahrain Al-Mousawi, 'When we spoke to Leila Alaoui on tackling taboos in art', Al Jazeera, 19 July 2015

title: Crossings

title: Dancer from the Peninsula
text: Over the course of my making Dancer from the Peninsula, Choi’s presence appeared to me slowly. She felt both familiar and distanced at the same time. Near the end of the working process, I observed that she had become split into both the subject and object of research.

title: Dancer from the Peninsula

text: Rooted in rich family history and ancestral memory, preserved through cherished oral storytelling and treasured heirlooms, this work constructs a compelling visual narrative. Through a combination of illustration and moving images, it vividly reimagines the routes taken by these ancestors, mapping not only the geographical landscapes they traversed but also the profound emotional experiences that shaped their arrival in Singapore.
speaker: Singapore Night Festival 2025 (programme text)
source: Singapore Night Festival 2025 programme page (archived)

title: Dari Pulau Ke Pulau (From One Island to Another)
text: I also reference a lot of archival photos - mostly from my own family when I draw my characters.

title: Dari Pulau Ke Pulau (From One Island to Another)

title: Das avós
text: The project was basically born from that idea of affection, and also from my reflecting on how important the issue of ancestry was, and still is, for the black population, I thought that viewing them as distant relatives would be a great work of personal and collective healing.

source: Statement 2019 (transcription of the statement for the 21st Biennial), Videobrasil archive

title: Das avós

title: Das avós

title: Datum Point
text: He once wrote that writing a poem is like kneading clay. There’s a very physical resistance—you have to push through it. That idea of kneading, of wrestling with a lump of language, really stayed with me. Writing felt like a material struggle, and clay gave me a way to embody that in animation.
speaker: Ryo Orikasa
source: Cartoon Brew, Animating Poetry (Chris Robinson)

title: Datum Point
text: No voice came to mind. There are recordings of him reciting his work, but I always felt that he wasn’t especially interested in performance. So for Datum Point, silence felt right. If I had forced a voice onto it, it would have betrayed that initial experience of reading—of not hearing.
speaker: Ryo Orikasa
source: Cartoon Brew, Animating Poetry (Chris Robinson)

title: Datum Point
text: I think of the act of making the film as one continuous event, and the finished film is simply a recording of that event.
speaker: Ryo Orikasa
source: Cartoon Brew, Animating Poetry (Chris Robinson)

title: Datum Point
text: I was interested in this film in the idea of a resistance to writing, of a resistance to something physical. In order to convey this motif of resisting the physical, in this case the physical act of writing, it seemed to me that the plasticity of clay could manifest this resistance to the physical more effectively than the act of writing on paper.
speaker: Ryo Orikasa
source: Annecy 2016 Shorts & Breakfast, transcript on Backpacking Japan blog

title: Datum Point

title: Dead Drops

title: FEARDEATHLOVEDEATH

For things to not get too abstract, I divided it into chapters: a dead person’s room, a time-based abstract painting in the style of Stan Brakhage, a love poem, and an alligator looking down from the clouds.

title: Homo Machina (Human Machine, a.k.a. Gay Machine)
text: We are on the edge of a new era. If technology is the medium of the future, it cannot be separated from class, fantasy, labor, and the body. As tech aesthetics grow more minimal, more polished, more sterile, something disappears: the messy, excessive, expressive relationships to technology that once offered pleasure, identity, and power. Homo Machina is my refusal of that disappearance.
speaker: Gabriela Ruiz
source: Whitney Biennial 2026 audio guide, transcription

title: Homo Machina (Human Machine, a.k.a. Gay Machine)

title: Homo Machina (Human Machine, a.k.a. Gay Machine)
text: For me, the machine is never neutral. It is fantasy—glamour, transformation, seduction—but it is also a tool through which violence is enacted. Surveillance, policing, extraction, and control are not side effects of technology; they are among its central functions. They shape who is seen, who is tracked, who is disciplined, who is allowed to move freely.
speaker: Gabriela Ruiz
source: Whitney Biennial 2026 audio guide, transcription

title: Homo Machina (Human Machine, a.k.a. Gay Machine)

title: Homo Machina (Human Machine, a.k.a. Gay Machine)
text: Homo Machina does not imagine escape from the machine. It stages the condition of being inside it—where bodies are expected to perform endlessly, to carry what others refuse to hold, and to survive within fantasies that remain seductive, yet ultimately unreachable.

source: Whitney Biennial 2026 audio guide, transcription

title: In Potentia

title: In Potentia

title: In Potentia

speaker: Guy Ben-Ary and Kirsten Hudson
source: In Potentia, guybenary.com

title: In Potentia

source: Artist statement ('Depoimento'), Julia Mensch page, 21st Bienal Sesc_Videobrasil website

title: La vida en rojo
text: The revolution my grandparents fought for had a color, a manifest, a party. I believe that, today, there may be not only one, but several revolutions and utopias, multiplying themselves under different forms instead of a vertical, allegedly homogenous one.
speaker: Julia Mensch
source: Artist statement ('Depoimento'), Julia Mensch page, 21st Bienal Sesc_Videobrasil website

title: La vida en rojo
text: Reading recent political memories from a letter, a small note, an underlined book, give us the possibility to relate to our own acts and political context, to rethink the present we are creating with our decisions and through acts that may appear small or insignificant.
speaker: Julia Mensch
source: Artist statement ('Depoimento'), Julia Mensch page, 21st Bienal Sesc_Videobrasil website

title: La vida en rojo
text: A few years ago my grandparent’s TV started to not function so well. The variations of colours of the TV screen were transformed into different red and magenta tones. Not green or blue, but red. When we told them that the TV was not working well, they didn’t agree; for them it was still perfectly functioning. This anecdote gave the name to Life in Red, a long term project, which takes as starting point the private and political life of my grandparents
speaker: Julia Mensch (artist's portfolio)
source: Julia Mensch, Portfolio 2026 (PDF), juliamensch.com

title: Labor

title: Labor
text: Our microbiota is integral to who and what we are, and complicates any simplistic sense of self. Likewise, the smell of the perspiring body is not just a human scent, unless we are willing to redefine what we mean by human.

title: Laundry Nocturne
text: In a world saturated by ceaseless stimuli, I often ask whether urban media art can do more than dazzle—whether it might return us to a finer state of feeling. Sound, light or rhythm, I am drawn to small, almost imperceptible interventions: gestures slight enough to let perception open slowly, and encounters flourish naturally.
speaker: Kingsley Ng
source: ArtDog Istanbul, 'Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice' (interview with the artists and curators)

title: Laundry Nocturne
text: The central motif is fluttering laundry, which charts rhythms of everyday life in both cities. The accompanying audio is also grounded in the quotidian, with field recordings in night-time Hong Kong (which is day time Venice during which the exhibition opens), including tribute to those who prepare the city for tomorrow while most are asleep, and other sounds of intimate domesticity.
speaker: Kingsley Ng
source: ArtDog Istanbul, 'Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice' (interview with the artists and curators)

title: Laundry Nocturne
text: My work always revolves around the notion of impermanence. I don’t really see my practice as preservation or transformation. It is more like an acknowledgement of ephemerality and seizing a fleeting moment.
speaker: Kingsley Ng
source: ArtDog Istanbul, 'Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice' (interview with the artists and curators)

title: Laundry Nocturne
text: The laundry becomes a point of entry into a wider soundscape of nighttime labour: recordings from a wastewater treatment plant, a newspaper-printing facility and a postal sorting centre evoke the work that continues while much of the city sleeps
speaker: Kingsley Ng
source: The Art Newspaper, 'Hong Kong artists create a poetic moment in Venice' (4 November 2026)

title: Laundry Nocturne
text: Creating spaces for listening has always been at the core of my practice. This responsibility has now extended to artists, designers, and cultural workers in Ukraine. Maps and mapping serve as a means for us, as artists and designers, to continue this work of bearing witness to the brutality of war, even if unsuccessfully.

text: I have always been fascinated by Lagos bridges, especially pedestrian bridges. For a city that moves fast, and is filled with people in a hurry to be somewhere, these bridges quietly hold moments of pause, expression, and shared motion.
speaker: Yinka Bernie
source: Contemporary And (C&), 'Moving Parts: Yinka Bernie's Sonic Bridge Across Lagos', 26 Mar 2026 (text excerpted from Yinka Bernie's channels)

title: Moving Parts
text: That whole concept is how Moving Parts came to be; going to these different bridges, making videos, collecting sounds, eavesdropping on conversations, speaking to people. I just put everything together.
speaker: Yinka Bernie
source: OkayAfrica, 'What It's Like To... Run an Indie Record Company and Keep Vinyl Alive' (Emmanuel Esomnofu), 24 Nov 2025

title: Moving Parts
text: The bridge is one place that is not still; Lagos itself is not still at all, but the bridge… there’s always movement, there’s always people using this bridge to do different things. The common goal is they’re always moving. So I thought ‘what name would fit this idea?’ Moving Parts is something that stuck and I just concluded to say we’re all moving parts of society and this exhibition captures Lagos in this time.
speaker: Yinka Bernie
source: OkayAfrica, 'What It's Like To... Run an Indie Record Company and Keep Vinyl Alive' (Emmanuel Esomnofu), 24 Nov 2025

title: Music of the Spheres
text: It is a music box that I built taking the planets in the solar system as notes. Based on the position the planets had on the specific day that I started the work – on October 20 – I juxtaposed empty musical scores to create a composition.
speaker: Glenda León
source: '55th Venice Biennale, Exclusive Interview: Glenda Leon / Cuban Pavilion', Uprising Art, 2013 (Wayback Machine copy)

title: Music of the Spheres
text: I loved the idea the planets have sound. I thought it was great. The way they move and the speed they move produces music but we are not able to hear it. We miss things. We do not have the ability to listen.
speaker: Glenda León
source: '55th Venice Biennale, Exclusive Interview: Glenda Leon / Cuban Pavilion', Uprising Art, 2013 (Wayback Machine copy)

title: Music of the Spheres
text: My idea for Música de las Esferas comes from the Greeks, and mainly Pythagoras and Plato.
speaker: Glenda León
source: '55th Venice Biennale, Exclusive Interview: Glenda Leon / Cuban Pavilion', Uprising Art, 2013 (Wayback Machine copy)

title: Music of the Spheres
text: I like playing with materials that you do not listen to but you know there is sound on it.
speaker: Glenda León
source: '55th Venice Biennale, Exclusive Interview: Glenda Leon / Cuban Pavilion', Uprising Art, 2013 (Wayback Machine copy)

title: Music of the Spheres
text: Many religious texts agree that sound existed before anything else in the world, before light and matter. That’s why this piece is silent as a way of returning to that discarded essence of us all, our most profound being that is linked to the Universe. And shouldn’t Silence exist even before Sound? The sense of the work lies in the interstice between them.
speaker: Glenda León (artist's website)
source: Música de las esferas | Music of the spheres, work page, glenda-leon.com

title: Máquina Stella
text: This piece is part of an inquiry in mechanisms and circuits, into the boundaries between voltage, -tension or strength- and resistance, inside a specific system.
speaker: Marcela Armas
source: Máquina Stella, video description on Marcela Armas's Vimeo account

title: Máquina Stella
text: Balance boundaries regarding the available energy and the resistance of materials, underline the fragility of the system.
speaker: Marcela Armas
source: Máquina Stella, video description on Marcela Armas's Vimeo account

title: Máquina Stella
text: This machine has taken shape in tune with a line of thought about the movement of energy in the cosmos.
speaker: Marcela Armas
source: 'Maquina Stella | MARCELA ARMAS', video description, Laboratorio Arte Alameda YouTube channel, 28 February 2012 (translated from Spanish)

title: Máquina Stella
text: In this sense, the process of building the work involves a deep empathy related to my conception of the machine.
speaker: Marcela Armas
source: 'Maquina Stella | MARCELA ARMAS', video description, Laboratorio Arte Alameda YouTube channel, 28 February 2012 (translated from Spanish)

title: Máquina Stella
text: My exploration of the relationship between art and technique arises as a way of generating questions or thinking through ideas
speaker: Marcela Armas
source: Pablo Farneda, 'Entrevista a la artista e investigadora Marcela Armas', Ludión, Mexico City, October 2013 (translated from Spanish)

title: Máquinas Salvajes
text: It allows me to explore a universe in which these robotic beings exist and, through them, to scrutinize ideas around possible technologies that are distanced from the needs of the current economic system of extraction and consumption, and are much closer to the needs of ecosystems.
speaker: Jonathan Torres Rodríguez
source: Interview, Ding Magazine (Superrr), issue 5

title: Máquinas Salvajes
text: The idea is to make visible a series of biodegradable, machinic beings, to materialize fragments of their still non-existent form, and be able to perceive some of their characteristics – at least those that allow us to think about their possible existence and the way they exist, the way they die, and the way they reintegrate – and so move them away from the current system of extraction and linear use of resources, and bring them closer to the systems of what is alive.
speaker: Jonathan Torres Rodríguez
source: Interview, Ding Magazine (Superrr), issue 5

title: Máquinas Salvajes
text: Thus, these works, these artifacts, by emulating the way biological systems die, allow us to think of them as alive. I consider that in this act is an enormous potency and it leads me to profound conceptual questions: how do machines die, or in what way should technologies die? What poetics are hidden in the death of a machinic being?
speaker: Jonathan Torres Rodríguez
source: Interview, Ding Magazine (Superrr), issue 5

title: Máquinas Salvajes
text: If technological devices generate discourse and create knowledge (Deleuze), it is urgent to think of the nature of these technologies. What if machines could become compost? Compost that decomposes in the modern world and blends in with the leaves and bugs. How could we achieve it? What new processes would we need? How can we all conceive of such a thing?
speaker: Jonathan Torres Rodríguez
source: Project text, Ars Electronica Festival 2023

title: Máquinas Salvajes
text: Whenever we go somewhere, what we do is take things. We hardly ever stop to think about these ways we have, as a species, of relating to the rest of the world.
speaker: Jonathan Torres Rodríguez
source: La Nación (Costa Rica), Revista Dominical (translated from Spanish)

title: Nairobi Berries
text: When I was story-boarding the film, my main concern was to use the space to create a dream-like state and to make the audience occupy the space with the feeling that this created world is constantly happening around them. I wanted it to feel like a waking dream.
speaker: Ng'endo Mukii
source: 'Award Winner Interview: Ng'endo Mukii', Encounters Film Festival, words Isabella Coombes (archived)

title: Nairobi Berries
text: I tried to think of ways to use this 360 space, without creating a gimmick.
speaker: Ng'endo Mukii
source: 'Award Winner Interview: Ng'endo Mukii', Encounters Film Festival (archived)

title: Nairobi Berries
text: The ebb and flow of the city affects how and when we interact, we learn to socially slip around each other, and through backstreets to avoid traffic. We’re always twisting and turning. Culturally and creatively, I feel we do these things as well. Specifically in Nairobi Berries, I think the poetry and imagery I created reflect this.
speaker: Ng'endo Mukii
source: 'Award Winner Interview: Ng'endo Mukii', Encounters Film Festival (archived)

title: Nairobi Berries
text: The title, Nairobi Berries, is a play on words for us. We often talk of ‘Nairoberry’ which refers to our high rate of crimes and robbery. I was contemplating on the why of this culture, what we are seeking that creates pervasive hording and petty crime. These are the ‘fruits promised.’
speaker: Ng'endo Mukii
source: MIT Docubase, 'Nairobi Berries' project page (quoted statement, credited 'Ng’endo Mukii, Author')

title: Nairobi Berries
text: My Nairobi is an ode to my city, from a quietly visceral perspective. It uses the physical environments explored in VR to delve into the spirit of the people who inhabit the boundaries of its social walls.
speaker: Ng'endo Mukii (work statement)
source: Radiance VR, artist page 'Ngendo Mukii' – Nairobi Berries description (unsigned, first person)

title: Nanohana Heels - Healing Fukushima
text: Healing Fukushima (Nanohana Heels) was created to provoke deeper discussion and to encourage people to explore the use of land of Fukushima as a viable source of sustainable energy.
speaker: Sputniko!
source: '01 Greetings from the Airport', serialized essay, Wochi Kochi Magazine (Japan Foundation), April 2013 — English translation published by the Japan Foundation

title: Nanohana Heels - Healing Fukushima
text: I like to create works which can challenge preconceptions and inspire new ways of thinking.
speaker: Sputniko!
source: '01 Greetings from the Airport', serialized essay, Wochi Kochi Magazine (Japan Foundation), April 2013 — English translation published by the Japan Foundation

title: Nanohana Heels - Healing Fukushima
text: All my ideas are born of research, whether in the field of science or engineering, fashion design or art.
speaker: Sputniko!
source: '01 Greetings from the Airport', serialized essay, Wochi Kochi Magazine (Japan Foundation), April 2013 — English translation published by the Japan Foundation

title: Necomimi
text: People think that our bodies have limitations, but just imagine if we had organs that don’t exist, and could control that new body?
speaker: neurowear
source: 'About necomimi', neurowear project page (Wayback Machine, 31 December 2013)

title: Necomimi
text: We created new human organs that use a brainwave sensor.
speaker: neurowear
source: 'About necomimi', neurowear project page (Wayback Machine, 31 December 2013)

title: Necomimi
text: What will happen when people show their feelings even when they don’t express them?
speaker: neurowear
source: 'About necomimi', neurowear project page (Wayback Machine, 31 December 2013)

title: Necomimi
text: If this trend continues, wouldn't it ultimately lead to communication without language?
speaker: Kana Nakano (neurowear)
source: 'Blog → Twitter → Like! → Brain?', interview with Kana Nakano and Toshitaka Kamiya, Dentsu-ho, 21 October 2013 (translated from Japanese; English machine translation published by dentsu-ho.com)

title: Necomimi
text: But multilingual support is tough, so I thought we should create something that doesn't rely on language in the first place.
speaker: Kana Nakano (neurowear)
source: 'Blog → Twitter → Like! → Brain?', interview with Kana Nakano and Toshitaka Kamiya, Dentsu-ho, 21 October 2013 (translated from Japanese; English machine translation published by dentsu-ho.com)

title: Neo Geo City
text: What you try to do when you find a medium is find its strengths and its weaknesses. I found out that if you want to go really 3D realistic, the browser can’t handle it, so I thought, "Let's go the opposite way. Let's make it simple as possible. What can a browser do that a DVD player cannot do?"
speaker: Rafaël Rozendaal
source: Interview by Leigh Silver, Complex, February 2014

title: Neo Geo City
text: A website is a work that exists in a specific place, in its domain name. It’s a place that you can go to wherever you are, by typing the title of the work into your browser. It’s a public place that is non-local.
speaker: Rafaël Rozendaal
source: Interview by A Will Brown, Studio International, 2015

title: Neo Geo City
text: Because a website is a new format, we look for analogies to understand what it is. It’s not a movie, it’s not a game, it’s not a painting: it’s something between those three, I think.
speaker: Rafaël Rozendaal
source: Interview by A Will Brown, Studio International, 2015

title: Neo Geo City
text: That’s why I make moving images that have no beginning or end. You can look at them for a few seconds, or leave them on your screen for a year.
speaker: Rafaël Rozendaal
source: Interview by A Will Brown, Studio International, 2015

title: Neo Geo City
text: The idea is that the website is like liquid, or like a piece of gas,
speaker: Rafaël Rozendaal
source: Rhizome, "Rafaël Rozendaal's Liquid Websites" (quoting Rhizome's video interviews), 2013

title: Never real historians, always near poets
text: The video commissioned for Singapore Biennale 2019 Never real historians, always near poets (2019) was also an important one and allowed us to delve deep into ideas that we had been discussing for many years.
speaker: Vong Phaophanit and Claire Oboussier
source: Art & Market, 'Midpoint: Vong Phaophanit and Claire Oboussier', interview by Ian Tee (15 December 2023)

title: Never real historians, always near poets
text: We worked in a similar way to when we created our book in Berlin, Vong collected images and Claire wrote text and documented the stories that we were encountering. We brought the two elements together in an intuitive, poetic editing process. This is a way of working that we have continued to evolve for all our moving image works.
speaker: Vong Phaophanit and Claire Oboussier
source: Art & Market, 'Midpoint: Vong Phaophanit and Claire Oboussier', interview by Ian Tee (15 December 2023)

title: Never real historians, always near poets
text: In the end, it is about making sense of the world, about empathy, keeping the process of meaning-making alive, and resisting fixity.
speaker: Vong Phaophanit and Claire Oboussier
source: Art & Market, 'Midpoint: Vong Phaophanit and Claire Oboussier', interview by Ian Tee (15 December 2023)

title: Night Charades
text: The silence of this transmission—the absence of a soundtrack—led me to the idea of charade, which is a game as well as a performance in the warmth of a home. I am intrigued by the notion of transforming a game that is usually played within the confines of a home with friends and family into something not only extremely public but also distantly familiar yet alien.
speaker: Ho Tzu Nyen
source: M+ Magazine, 'Night Charades: Reimagining Hong Kong Cinema' (interview by Ariadne Long and Silke Schmickl)

title: Night Charades
text: The one question I asked and continue to ask myself is: ‘Who is this work for?’
speaker: Ho Tzu Nyen
source: M+ Magazine, 'Night Charades: Reimagining Hong Kong Cinema' (interview by Ariadne Long and Silke Schmickl)

title: Night Charades
text: But I’ve become increasingly troubled by the cruelty of decision that lies in the selection process of filmmaking—the selection of that one perfect angle, that one perfect moment, and that one perfect shot, to be placed in the one perfect sequence to obtain that perfect timeline. The final result is that one perfect film by the one singular auteur. However, what interests me, at this moment, is no longer this search for the ‘one’, but rather how we can create a system that can continuously generate multiple versions of itself, and how this multiplicity can be shaped, as form.
speaker: Ho Tzu Nyen
source: M+ Magazine, 'Night Charades: Reimagining Hong Kong Cinema' (interview by Ariadne Long and Silke Schmickl)

title: Night Charades
text: I was struck by how much of Hong Kong cinema and Cantopop were described as having their ‘Golden Ages’ in the 1980s and 1990s. Of course, I can understand why these are labelled as such, but this way of attributing an unsurpassable peak to past achievements nevertheless troubled me.
speaker: Ho Tzu Nyen
source: M+ Magazine, 'Night Charades: Reimagining Hong Kong Cinema' (interview by Ariadne Long and Silke Schmickl)

title: Night Charades
text: What I resist is the single version, the single timeline. AI is a way for me to work with multiple versions, which is to say that there is no perfect version, it’s always slightly imperfect, like a charade.
speaker: Ho Tzu Nyen
source: The Art Newspaper, 'Ho Tzu Nyen on how AI leads to the cinematic past' (interview)

title: No Bird
text: The origins of this work lay in imagining these now-vanished flightless birds. Perhaps they might have survived if their footsteps were erased?
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: No Bird, work description on the artists' blog, January 2026

title: No Bird
text: The repetitive cycle of these two machines—endlessly leaving and erasing—reveals a state in which action is continuously produced yet exhausted without leading to any change or direction.
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: No Bird, work description on the artists' blog, January 2026

title: No Bird
text: This serves as a metaphor for the conditions of a post-automation society, where humans remain alive but exist as beings unable to intervene in the world.
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: No Bird, work description on the artists' blog, January 2026

title: No Bird
text: What vanishes is not only the flightless bird. What is disappearing is the human role, no longer summoned in a post-automation society, along with the conditions of meaning and dignity that humans have given to themselves.
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: Catalogue text, Prix Ars Electronica 2026 (Honorary Mention, Interactive Art +)

title: No Bird
text: Through its physical mechanical structure, No Bird asks what it means to exist as a human in a post-technological era, and how we might live beyond mere survival.
speaker: UJOO+LIMHEEYOUNG
source: Catalogue text, Prix Ars Electronica 2026 (Honorary Mention, Interactive Art +)

title: Norman
text: In 2017 I created a custom animation tool—for myself. A tool to enable and facilitate my imagination and flow.
speaker: James Paterson
source: Prix Ars Electronica archive, catalogue text (Computer Animation, Honorary Mention 2018)

title: Norman
text: It makes the process of animating more like playing a musical instrument. For instance, one mode automatically creates new frames and advances through the timeline each time you make a mark. The user can get completely lost in the process of drawing through time and space, without having to manually control the time-line.
speaker: James Paterson
source: Prix Ars Electronica archive, catalogue text

title: Norman
text: Norman is an experiment in building a medium and using that medium to create concrete works, at the same time.
speaker: James Paterson
source: Prix Ars Electronica archive, catalogue text

title: Norman
text: I have always been fascinated by the idea of our imaginations finding their way out of our minds and into concrete reality. Until virtual reality I pursued that interest by developing imagery with drawing, animation and code. For ages I have been waiting for virtual reality to mature so that I can create and hang out in imaginary worlds. And, even more importantly, make and use tools to create within these worlds where the laws of physics and normality do not apply.
speaker: James Paterson
source: British Council Voices magazine, 'How do virtual reality animators find communities and audiences?' (15 December 2017), Wayback Machine copy

title: Norman
text: One of the most interesting things about code as a medium is that it allows us to operate on a meta-level: not only can we dream up solutions using the tools we already have, but we can also dream up and build new tools as we go.
speaker: James Paterson
source: Transform magazine, 'Five minutes with James Paterson' (2020)

title: NoSearchBar
text: A distinction can be made between specific and non-specific software-related data access: The specific search hardly has any surprises in store, due to its purpose of existence. We find what we are looking for, the problems, preferences, and needs are specifically individual, predominantly environmental, and self-driven.
speaker: Erik Anton Reinhardt
source: Prix Ars Electronica 2022 winners page, project text (archived)

title: NoSearchBar
text: Examples of this are forecast systems, sorting, categories, and recommendation systems, which try to anticipate users’ problems, preferences, and needs but often also to create new ones.
speaker: Erik Anton Reinhardt
source: Prix Ars Electronica 2022 winners page, project text (archived)

title: NoSearchBar
text: By removing the SearchBar, we are exposed to an ideological software anticipation. We no longer have the opportunity to articulate our own problems, preferences, and needs but are always left with mixed feelings between frustration and hope that the right thing could still emerge.
speaker: Erik Anton Reinhardt
source: Prix Ars Electronica 2022 winners page, project text (archived)

title: NoSearchBar
text: The specific access is reflected in the way we articulate ourselves through using a SearchBar. We find the answers to our needs and problems that are driven by an individual's desires.
speaker: Erik Anton Reinhardt
source: UdK Berlin New Media Class, student project page

title: Not Your World Music: Noise in South East Asia
text: The book — just as my essays and talks — is partly there to disprove this myth. And the title is clear about it. Most noise artists don’t use traditional elements in their music, wherever they live on Earth, so why would Asians or Africans break the rule to fit their ex-colonizers’ expectations?
speaker: Cedrik Fermont
source: Zuzana Friday, 'Digging the Asian and African undergrounds with C-drík Kirdec', CDM Create Digital Music (August 2016)

title: Not Your World Music: Noise in South East Asia
text: I think it would be hard to understand why noise music exists or not somewhere without historical and socio-political and sometimes religious or philosophical context.
speaker: Cedrik Fermont
source: Zuzana Friday, 'Digging the Asian and African undergrounds with C-drík Kirdec', CDM Create Digital Music (August 2016)

title: Not Your World Music: Noise in South East Asia
text: It is partly the result of a frustration and partly the result of many years of exploration, research, travels and discussions.
speaker: Cedrik Fermont
source: 'Interview with Cedrik Fermont (C-Drik) about Less Familiar Underground Scenes In The World', Side-Line (2016)

title: Not Your World Music: Noise in South East Asia
text: I think that all my researches, travels, explorations, publications and releases about Asian and Africa come from the fact that I am tired to always hear the same non-sense: ‘There’s nothing there’ or ‘We – the West – invented everything before them’ or ‘They just copy music from the West’, etc.
speaker: Cedrik Fermont
source: 'Interview with Cedrik Fermont (C-Drik) about Less Familiar Underground Scenes In The World', Side-Line (2016)

title: Not Your World Music: Noise in South East Asia
text: This compilation is an attempt to cover a varied range of noise and experimental music from South East Asia. Limited to just over one hour, the CD format does not allow us to fully cover the richness of the scene. However, we did our best to include a diverse group of artists. We have selected female and male artists, DIY and academically trained musicians, and newcomers and established artists.
speaker: Cedrik Fermont and Dimitri della Faille (project website)
source: Not Your World Music, 'Companion compilation' page, words.hushush.com

title: Nothing to See Here
text: We playfully challenge you to consider what is true or real, and whether we can ever truly know.
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Statement on Nothing to see here, Studio Nergens website (English version)

title: Nothing to See Here
text: Fragmented truths in endless doomscrolling, AI videos of cute but non-existent cats, fake news reports – reality is not one fixed fact, but something relational that comes into being in the interaction between our body, the other and the space,
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Quoted in 'Nothing to see here', Creative Industries Fund NL project page

title: Nothing to See Here
text: By literally positioning someone opposite themselves, I hope to force the audience to rethink that relationship for a moment.
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Quoted in 'Nothing to see here', Creative Industries Fund NL project page

title: Nothing to See Here
text: To see a group of strangers of different ages and backgrounds having a chat and while doing so asking the question whether we actually agree on what is real, I find that moving and important in these times,
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Quoted in 'Nothing to see here', Creative Industries Fund NL project page

title: Nothing to See Here
text: I hope a lot more people will put their heads into this peep-show box for a moment, only to emerge somewhat confused and dazed. That they look at the world around them with new eyes.
speaker: Celine Daemen
source: Quoted in 'Nothing to see here', Creative Industries Fund NL project page

title: Now he's out in public and everyone can see
text: is an 18-channel video installation on collective performances of race and racial anxiety in the Obama era. A 16-minute narrative samples from hundreds of online vlogs that narrate and editorialize on a series of viral media scandals involving famous African American men.
speaker: Natalie Bookchin (artist's website)
source: Now he's out in public and everyone can see, project page, bookchin.net (Wayback Machine copy, 2015)

title: Now he's out in public and everyone can see
text: Weaving the various scandals and rumors together and removing the names suggest that the specifics don’t really matter. The man in question is a figment of the speakers’ and the viewers’ imaginations, composed of rumours and gossip, speculations, and judgements. The language and the stories themselves keep repeating — different man, different incident, but same old story.
speaker: Natalie Bookchin
source: 'Natalie Bookchin in Conversation with Alexandra Juhasz: Performances of Race and White Hegemony on YouTube', in Fabricating Publics, eds. Bill Balaskas and Carolina Rito (Open Humanities Press, 2021), PDF on bookchin.net

title: Now he's out in public and everyone can see
text: The work explores how antagonistic performances of race and white dominance were a significant part of online spaces like YouTube even in its infancy.
speaker: Natalie Bookchin
source: 'Natalie Bookchin in Conversation with Alexandra Juhasz: Performances of Race and White Hegemony on YouTube', in Fabricating Publics, eds. Bill Balaskas and Carolina Rito (Open Humanities Press, 2021), PDF on bookchin.net

title: Now he's out in public and everyone can see
text: What it boils down to in each of these so-called scandals, is that to be a Black man and in public is the scandal.
speaker: Natalie Bookchin
source: 'Natalie Bookchin in Conversation with Alexandra Juhasz: Performances of Race and White Hegemony on YouTube', in Fabricating Publics, eds. Bill Balaskas and Carolina Rito (Open Humanities Press, 2021), PDF on bookchin.net

title: Now he's out in public and everyone can see
text: The installation of Now he’s out in public conjures a mass that is fragmented and dispersed — a reality shattered into shards of opinions. There is no centre, no shared or agreed upon truth.
speaker: Natalie Bookchin
source: 'Natalie Bookchin in Conversation with Alexandra Juhasz: Performances of Race and White Hegemony on YouTube', in Fabricating Publics, eds. Bill Balaskas and Carolina Rito (Open Humanities Press, 2021), PDF on bookchin.net

title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't
text: Puddles are humble, beautiful things, and they used to have a longer life on Earth
speaker: Manal AlDowayan
source: The National, 'Saudi artist Manal AlDowayan unveils new piece of land art addressing water scarcity in Al Ula' (2020)

title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't
text: Al Ula was founded because it had plentiful springs, it was this oasis in the desert, but as the climate changed these local communities had to start tapping into the underground reserves, so even when it does rain, puddles disappear almost instantly.
speaker: Manal AlDowayan
source: The National (2020)

title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't
text: I wanted kids to engage, as they might jump in a puddle. At night the work is up-lit and appears as strange black pools. People are nervous at first, but I've seen young and old now have a go.
speaker: Manal AlDowayan
source: The National (2020)

title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't
text: I work in a lot of different media, my projects always take different forms, and have different politics, but ideas of disappearance and invisibility run through everything I do.
speaker: Manal AlDowayan
source: The National (2020)

title: Nuestra Victoria (Our Victory)
text: The work consists of a 3D digital archive that intends to preserve the data of the monument after its occupation by civil society.
speaker: Julieta Gil
source: Nuestra Victoria, project text on the artist's website

title: Nuestra Victoria (Our Victory)
text: The intention was not to make a perfect replica, but to also allow the materiality of this digital version to show through and reveal new layers of information about its process of preservation and restoration, and allow the mistakes and imperfections of the scan to serve as a metaphor for the fragility of patriarchal institutions.
speaker: Julieta Gil
source: Nuestra Victoria, project text on the artist's website

title: Nuestra Victoria (Our Victory)
text: Hours after the protest, government censorship prevented people from seeing the Angel of Independence by boarding it up and immediately working on its restoration, thus erasing all the claims against violence that were posted by women all over the monument. This work allows the words and actions of protest to remain in our collective memory.
speaker: Julieta Gil
source: Lumen Prize Gold Award winner 2020, work description

title: Nuit Blanche
artist: Arev Manoukian, Marc-André Gray (National Film Board of Canada)
text: The idea for Nuit Blanche came from the notion of having a special moment with a total stranger, which happens to everyone, especially in a large metropolitan city. It lasts for a split second, then things get awkward, so we turn away. I wanted to take that moment of attraction and stretch it in a hyper‐real fantasy where things unfold like slow-moving photographs.
speaker: Arev Manoukian
source: Quoted in Justice Mitchell, "Exploding Noir At 2,000 Frames Per Second" (blog post), 2010

title: Nuit Blanche
artist: Arev Manoukian, Marc-André Gray (National Film Board of Canada)
text: For 3-D we used Maya and mental ray, 3ds Max and V-Ray,
speaker: Arev Manoukian
source: Quoted in Justice Mitchell, "Exploding Noir At 2,000 Frames Per Second" (blog post), 2010

title: Nyctinasty
text: It references both bodily and symbolic practices of caring for the body and spirit after death, forging a vital link between the living and the dead.
speaker: Hayley Millar Baker
source: Nyctinasty, artist's website

title: Nyctinasty
text: In this context, death is seen not as an end but as a continuation within the spiritual realm, reflecting a timeless link to ancestral wisdom and spiritual continuity.
speaker: Hayley Millar Baker
source: Nyctinasty, artist's website

title: Nyctinasty

title: Oceans in Transformation

title: Oceans in Transformation

title: OPERA

title: OPERA

title: REPETAE

title: REPETAE
text: So much dialogue around creative AI has to do with appropriation, copying, imitation, and how such "repetition" can never be authentic. title: REPETAE

title: REPETAE

text: I’ve always been drawn to building spaces rather than objects. I’m interested in how we can experience art through the body—through rest, slowness, or stillness. In Sangeh Khara, viewers lie down under a canopy of melhifa fabric, surrounded by sound and light. The installation echoes nomadic architecture in the oases, where shade is essential. I wanted to offer a space that envelops the viewer—a place to breathe, to see differently.

title: Screen Melancholy
text: Within the counterbalance of exhaustion, tension and collision, a narrative slowly emerges. In contemporary image production, artists inevitably rely on lots of different software tools. Some are open-source and free, while others are highly commercial. Each choice represents a different possibility for expression, but also has its own limitations and controls. I move among these systems, trying to grasp the subtle relationship of dependence and resistance between artists and contemporary tools. Through this process, using these image production techniques, I contemplate the state of humankind in relation to technological media.
speaker: Li Yi-Fan

title: SEA STATE
text: I am inverting the way we look at water. Water is often seen as a barricade. Somehow, the dominant myth about it is that if you fall into the water, you only have 15 seconds – or something like that – to live, before hypothermia kicks in. But in the tropics, the temperature of water is near to the temperature of our blood. Water is actually safe; it is a space where one may seek refuge in case of a storm.

title: SEA STATE
